title: Luqman's counsel, whole
hook: a father's advice to his son (31:12–19)
tomorrow: why would God make people into different tribes at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the servants of the Merciful: they walk gently, and answer the rude with Peace whether or not it lands. Today a father puts that same gentleness into words for his son.

Somebody in every family group chat types in all caps. Surah Luqman ends a father's advice on exactly that. The Qur'an says Luqman was given wisdom, and here he is, not preaching to a crowd, just talking to his own son. The advice starts with God, then moves through parents and patience and pride, and the very last line is about volume. In Pickthall's words: "Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice."
screen: `ALL CAPS.` → `A WISE FATHER, TALKING.` → `SUBDUE THY VOICE.`

segments.voice: It opens at the top: "O my dear son! Ascribe no partners unto Allah." Then God's own voice breaks in about parents: a mother carries her child "in weakness upon weakness"; be grateful to Me and to your parents. Even if parents push you to set partners beside God, don't obey that, but keep their company kindly in this world. Back to Luqman. A deed the weight of a mustard seed, hidden in a rock or in the heavens, God brings it out. "O my dear son! Establish worship," call to good, stop what's wrong, be patient with what comes. "Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land." And then the voice: lower it. The harshest of voices, the verse ends, is the donkey's bray, a homely picture, and it's right there in the text. Here's the detail to tell someone tonight: the counsel climbs all the way from God down to the volume of a sentence, and treats both as wisdom. Now hold this week up beside it. Young men at a cave asking for right conduct. A teacher whose damage hid mercy. A procession of the merciful. A barefoot man asking for a loosened tongue. A lamp beside the dark. Servants who walk gently. Luqman would have recognized every one.
screen: `FROM GOD ALONE.` · `KINDNESS TO PARENTS, NOT BLIND OBEDIENCE.` · `A MUSTARD SEED, BROUGHT OUT.` · `A WEEK OF WHOLE PASSAGES.` · then, large: `LOWER YOUR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Make a small plan for a conversation you're dreading: name what you want from it, and name the moment your voice will start to rise. Then choose what you'll do when it does: a breath, a slower sentence, the same words said lower. Hold that plan through the sit. And if there's a young person in your life, this is a passage worth reading to them one day.

fork.setup: your friend's parents push her to give up what she believes about God. by Luqman's surah, what does she still owe them?
options: full obedience: parents come before everything, even this.
kindness and good company in this world, without obeying that push.
nothing at all: she can cut them off for good.
fork.reveal: 31:15 holds both: don't obey a push to set partners beside God, and keep company with them kindly in this world.

options: Luqman: subdue thy voice. Say all of it, just lower. That's not backing down.
Say nothing. Respect means a child just listens; Luqman's son never spoke.
Get loud so he hears it. Luqman's advice was about strangers, not dads.
chat.meaning: Luqman's counsel ends on a lowered voice, not a silenced one. The point is the volume, not swallowing what you need to say.
